claim: Mice fed a Western diet (WD) for 2 weeks showed significant and prolonged hypothermia starting at 10 hr post-LPS injection compared to standard chow (SC)-fed mice.
source: WD- and KD-fed mice showed significant and prolonged hypothermia, starting at 10 hr post-injection (p.i.), compared to the SC-fed mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A measuring temperature loss in mice fed different diets after LPS injection.

claim: Mice fed a ketogenic diet (KD) for 2 weeks showed significant and prolonged hypothermia starting at 10 hr post-LPS injection compared to standard chow (SC)-fed mice.
source: WD- and KD-fed mice showed significant and prolonged hypothermia, starting at 10 hr post-injection (p.i.), compared to the SC-fed mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A measuring temperature loss in mice fed different diets after LPS injection.

claim: WD-fed mice displayed 100% mortality by 26 hr post-LPS injection compared to 100% survival of SC-fed mice.
source: In accordance with these findings, WD- and KD-fed mice displayed 100% mortality by 26 hr p.i. compared to 100% survival of SC-fed mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B comparing mortality rates between diet groups.

claim: KD-fed mice displayed 100% mortality by 26 hr post-LPS injection compared to 100% survival of SC-fed mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B comparing mortality rates between diet groups.

claim: Hypoglycemia is a known driver of endotoxemia.
source: Hypoglycemia is a known driver of endotoxemia, and each of these diets has varying levels of sugars and carbohydrates (Supplementary file 1; Raetzsch et al., 2009; Filkins and Cornell, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Raetzsch et al., 2009; Filkins and Cornell, 1974).

claim: Mice in all diet groups displayed similar levels of LPS-induced hypoglycemia during disease.
source: However, mice in all diet groups displayed similar levels of LPS-induced hypoglycemia during disease (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that potential effects of diet on blood glucose were not a driver of enhanced disease severity.
evidence: The claim is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Potential effects of diet on blood glucose were not a driver of enhanced disease severity in WD- and KD-fed mice.
source: However, mice in all diet groups displayed similar levels of LPS-induced hypoglycemia during disease (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that potential effects of diet on blood glucose were not a driver of enhanced disease severity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that all diet groups showed similar hypoglycemia despite different disease outcomes.

claim: At 5 hr post-LPS injection, WD-fed mice experienced significantly higher expression of Tnf in the blood compared with SC-fed mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C measuring Tnf expression.

claim: Mice exposed to diets enriched in SFAs show an initial hyper-inflammatory response to LPS, followed by an increased immunoparalytic phenotype, which correlates with enhanced disease severity.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of early hyper-inflammation and late immunoparalysis in SFA-fed mice.

claim: WD-fed mice experience increased endotoxemia severity and mortality, independent of diet-associated microbiome.

evidence: The claim is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 1H for germ-free mice.

claim: Il10 expression was not significantly different between WD-, KD-, and SC-fed GF mice throughout the time course.
source: Interestingly, Il10 expression and the Il10:Tnf ratio were not significantly different throughout all diets, suggesting the SFA-dependent enhanced immunoparalytic phenotype is dependent on the diet-associated microbiomes in WD- and KD-fed mice (Figure 1M–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1M measuring Il10 expression in germ-free mice.

claim: The Il10:Tnf ratio was not significantly different between WD-, KD-, and SC-fed GF mice throughout the time course.

claim: The SFA-dependent enhanced immunoparalytic phenotype is dependent on the diet-associated microbiomes in WD- and KD-fed mice.

evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing conventional and germ-free mouse data showing similar early inflammation but different late immunoparalysis.

claim: The late immunoparalytic response to LPS associated with enriched dietary SFAs is not independent of the diet-dependent microbiota.

evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing conventional and germ-free mouse data showing different late immunoparalysis patterns.

claim: Trained immunity is an innate immune memory response characterized by reprogramming of myeloid cells by a primary inflammatory stimulus, that then responds more robustly to secondary inflammatory challenge.
source: Specifically, trained immunity is an innate immune memory response characterized by reprogramming of myeloid cells by a primary inflammatory stimulus, that then responds more robustly to secondary inflammatory challenge.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about trained immunity.

claim: 4 weeks of WD feeding in Ldlr−/− mice significantly enhances multipotent progenitors (MPPs) and granulocyte and monocyte precursors (GMPs).
source: A previous study in Ldlr−/− mice has shown 4 weeks of WD feeding significantly enhances multipotent progenitors (MPPs) and granulocyte and monocyte precursors (GMPs) and skews development of GMPs toward a monocyte lineage that is primed to respond with a hyper-inflammatory response to LPS (Christ et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Christ et al., 2018).

claim: 4 weeks of WD feeding in Ldlr−/− mice skews development of GMPs toward a monocyte lineage that is primed to respond with a hyper-inflammatory response to LPS.
source: A previous study in Ldlr−/− mice has shown 4 weeks of WD feeding significantly enhances multipotent progenitors (MPPs) and granulocyte and monocyte precursors (GMPs) and skews development of GMPs toward a monocyte lineage that is primed to respond with a hyper-inflammatory response to LPS (Christ et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Christ et al., 2018).

claim: KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced short-term HSCs (ST-HSCs) compared to SC-fed mice.
source: Strikingly, we find that KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced ST- and LT-HSCs, and MPPs compared to SC-fed mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C quantifying HSC populations.

claim: KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs) compared to SC-fed mice.

claim: KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced multipotent progenitors (MPPs) compared to SC-fed mice.

claim: There was no significant change in ST-HSCs, LT-HSCs, or MPPs within WD-fed WT mice.
source: Unlike previously reported in Ldlr−/− mice, there was no significant change in ST-HSCs, LT-HSCs, or MPPs within WD-fed WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C showing no significant differences for WD-fed mice.

claim: The KD, a diet solely enriched in SFAs, alters hematopoiesis by enhancing expansion and differentiation of HSCs.
source: These data are the first to show that the KD, a diet solely enriched in SFAs, alters hematopoiesis by enhancing expansion and differentiation of HSCs, similar to previously described inducers of trained immunity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that KD feeding increased HSC populations similar to known trained immunity inducers.

claim: BMDMs from KD-fed mice showed significantly higher secretion of TNF when stimulated with LPS for 24 hr ex vivo compared to BMDMs from SC-fed mice.
source: However, when BMDMs were stimulated with LPS for 24 hr ex vivo, BMDMs from WD- and KD-fed mice showed significantly higher secretion of TNF, and only those from KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced IL-6 secretion (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2D measuring TNF secretion from BMDMs.

claim: BMDMs from WD-fed mice showed significantly higher secretion of TNF when stimulated with LPS for 24 hr ex vivo compared to BMDMs from SC-fed mice.

claim: BMDMs from KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced IL-6 secretion when stimulated with LPS for 24 hr ex vivo compared to BMDMs from SC-fed mice.

claim: Diets enriched in SFAs induce long-lasting inflammatory reprogramming of myeloid cells in vivo.
source: These data show that diets enriched in SFAs are inducing long-lasting inflammatory reprogramming of myeloid cells in vivo, and that reprogramming takes place within the bone marrow.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BMDMs isolated from SFA-fed mice and cultured for 7 days still showed enhanced inflammatory responses.

claim: Reprogramming of myeloid cells by diets enriched in SFAs takes place within the bone marrow.
source: These data show that diets enriched in SFAs are inducing long-lasting inflammatory reprogramming of myeloid cells in vivo, and that reprogramming takes place within the bone marrow.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that bone marrow-derived cells showed enhanced inflammatory responses after ex vivo culture.

claim: BMMs from KD-fed mice showed significantly higher expression of Tnf when stimulated with LPS for 2 hr ex vivo compared to BMMs from SC-fed mice.
source: However, when BMMs were stimulated with LPS for 2 hr ex vivo, those from KD-fed mice showed significantly higher expression of Tnf and Il6, while those from WD-fed mice exhibited no significance in expression compared to SC-fed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D measuring Tnf expression in BMMs.

claim: BMMs from KD-fed mice showed significantly higher expression of Il6 when stimulated with LPS for 2 hr ex vivo compared to BMMs from SC-fed mice.
source: However, when BMMs were stimulated with LPS for 2 hr ex vivo, those from KD-fed mice showed significantly higher expression of Tnf and Il6, while those from WD-fed mice exhibited no significance in expression compared to SC-fed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D measuring Il6 expression in BMMs.

claim: Splenocytes from KD-fed mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Tnf when challenged with LPS (2 hr) compared to splenocytes from SC-fed mice.
source: Similarly, we isolated splenocytes from SC-, WD-, and KD-fed mice and found no difference between homeostatic inflammation of splenocytes between diets, but a significantly enhanced expression of Tnf in the splenocytes of KD-fed mice, and not WD-fed mice, challenged with LPS (2 hr) compared to splenocytes from SC-fed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F measuring Tnf expression in splenocytes.

claim: The KD stimulates expansion of HSC populations and skew differentiation of myeloid progenitors that then give rise to macrophages with enhanced inflammatory potency.
source: These data show the KD stimulates expansion of HSC populations and skew differentiation of myeloid progenitors that then give rise to macrophages with enhanced inflammatory potency (Figure 2A–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of increased HSCs and enhanced inflammatory responses in KD-derived cells.

claim: BMDMs, BMMs, and splenocytes from WD- and KD-fed mice are not more inflammatory at homeostasis.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that BMDMs, BMMs, and splenocytes from WD- and KD-fed mice are not more inflammatory at homeostasis; however, when challenged with LPS, KD feeding confers a hyper-inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no significant differences in baseline cytokine expression in cells from different diet groups.

claim: When challenged with LPS, KD feeding confers a hyper-inflammatory response in BMDMs, BMMs, and splenocytes.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that BMDMs, BMMs, and splenocytes from WD- and KD-fed mice are not more inflammatory at homeostasis; however, when challenged with LPS, KD feeding confers a hyper-inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing enhanced cytokine expression in KD-derived cells after LPS challenge.

claim: The KD leads to reprogramming of the HSC compartment and long-lasting trained immunity.
source: Together, our results suggest the KD, a diet that comprised 90.5% SFAs, leads to reprogramming of the HSC compartment and long-lasting trained immunity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of HSC changes and persistent inflammatory reprogramming in KD-fed mice.

claim: The SFAs consumed in the diet determine the SFA profiles in the blood.
source: It is known that the SFAs consumed in the diet determine the SFA profiles in the blood (Dougherty et al., 1987; Skeaff et al., 2006; Zöllner and Tatò, 1992), and that these SFAs have the potential to be immunomodulatory.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dougherty et al., 1987; Skeaff et al., 2006; Zöllner and Tatò, 1992).

claim: Dietary SFAs have the potential to be immunomodulatory.
source: It is known that the SFAs consumed in the diet determine the SFA profiles in the blood (Dougherty et al., 1987; Skeaff et al., 2006; Zöllner and Tatò, 1992), and that these SFAs have the potential to be immunomodulatory.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about the immunomodulatory properties of SFAs.

claim: 2 weeks of KD feeding are sufficient to alter circulating FFAs, TAGs, and PCs.
source: These data indicate that 2 weeks of KD feeding are sufficient to alter circulating FFAs, TAGs, and PCs, and that SC- and KD-fed mice display unique lipid blood profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis showing distinct clustering of lipid profiles between SC and KD groups.

claim: SC- and KD-fed mice display unique lipid blood profiles.
source: These data indicate that 2 weeks of KD feeding are sufficient to alter circulating FFAs, TAGs, and PCs, and that SC- and KD-fed mice display unique lipid blood profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A-C showing no overlap between SC and KD groups.

claim: There was a significant increase in free palmitic acid (PA; C16:0) in KD-fed mice compared to SC-fed mice.
source: Interestingly, in KD-fed mice we found a significant increase in free PA (C16:0), an immunomodulatory SFA that is found naturally in animal fats, vegetable oils, and human breast milk (Mancini et al., 2015) and is eightfold enriched in KD (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3D comparing PA levels between SC and KD groups.

claim: PA is an immunomodulatory SFA that is found naturally in animal fats, vegetable oils, and human breast milk.
source: Interestingly, in KD-fed mice we found a significant increase in free PA (C16:0), an immunomodulatory SFA that is found naturally in animal fats, vegetable oils, and human breast milk (Mancini et al., 2015) and is eightfold enriched in KD (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Mancini et al., 2015).

claim: PA is eightfold enriched in KD compared to SC.
source: Interestingly, in KD-fed mice we found a significant increase in free PA (C16:0), an immunomodulatory SFA that is found naturally in animal fats, vegetable oils, and human breast milk (Mancini et al., 2015) and is eightfold enriched in KD (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by diet composition data provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: PA-containing TAGs were significantly elevated in KD-fed mice serum compared to SC-fed mice.
source: Additionally, PA-containing TAGs and PCs were significantly elevated in KD-fed mice serum, compared to SC-fed mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PA-containing PCs were significantly elevated in KD-fed mice serum compared to SC-fed mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: KD feeding enhances the frequency PA is incorporated into other lipid species in the blood.
source: These data indicate that KD feeding not only enhances levels of freely circulating PA, but also enhances the frequency PA is incorporated into other lipid species in the blood.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both free PA and PA-containing lipids were elevated in KD-fed mice.

claim: PA alone induces a modest, but highly reproducible increase in the expression and release of inflammatory cytokines in macrophages and monocytes.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lancaster et al., 2018; Korbecki and Bajdak-Rusinek, 2019).

claim: A wide range of serum PA levels, between 0.3 and 4.1 mM, reflects a high-fat diet in humans.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Abdelmagid et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Gallego et al., 2018; Buchanan et al., 2021; Perreault et al., 2014).

claim: BMDMs pre-treated with PA (1 mM) for 12 hr expressed significantly higher levels of Tnf in response to secondary treatment with LPS compared to naïve BMDMs.

claim: BMDMs pre-treated with PA (1 mM) for 12 hr expressed significantly higher levels of Il6 in response to secondary treatment with LPS compared to naïve BMDMs.

claim: Secretion of TNF was enhanced in BMDMs pre-treated with PA (1 mM) for 12 hr and challenged with LPS.

evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3H measuring TNF secretion.

claim: Secretion of IL-6 was enhanced in BMDMs pre-treated with PA (1 mM) for 12 hr and challenged with LPS.
source: Il1b expression was significantly lower in cells pre-treated with PA (Figure 3G); however, secretion of TNF, IL-6, and IL-1β was enhanced in BMDMs pre-treated with PA (1 mM) for 12 hr and challenged with LPS (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3I measuring IL-6 secretion.

claim: Secretion of IL-1β was enhanced in BMDMs pre-treated with PA (1 mM) for 12 hr and challenged with LPS.

claim: PA pre-treatment of macrophages induces a hyper-inflammatory response to LPS independent of cell death.

claim: PA is sensitizing macrophages to secondary inflammatory challenge.
source: These data demonstrate PA pre-treatment of macrophages induces a hyper-inflammatory response to LPS independent of cell death, suggesting PA is sensitizing macrophages to secondary inflammatory challenge.

claim: Both 12- and 24-hr pre-treatments with 0.5 mM or 1 mM of PA conjugated to 2% BSA are sufficient to induce reprogramming of macrophages and alter the response to stimulation with a heterologous ligand.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing enhanced inflammatory responses after different PA treatment durations and concentrations.

claim: PA treatment of various cell types diverts cellular metabolism toward the synthesis of the toxic metabolic byproducts: diacylglycerols and ceramide.

claim: BMDMs pre-treated simultaneously with PA and FB1 for 12 hr expressed significantly lower levels of IL-6 secretion in response to LPS compared to BMDMs pre-treated with only PA.

claim: BMDMs pre-treated simultaneously with PA and FB1 for 12 hr expressed significantly lower levels of IL-1β secretion in response to LPS compared to BMDMs pre-treated with only PA.

claim: Ceramide synthesis induced by PA is required for the macrophage hyper-inflammatory response to secondary challenge with LPS.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that inhibiting ceramide synthesis with FB1 reduced PA-induced hyper-inflammation.

claim: A 750-mM i.p. injection of ethyl palmitate enhances free PA levels in the serum to 173–425 μM compared to Veh-treated mice with 110–250 μM.
source: Similar to previous publications, we find that a 750-mM i.p. injection of ethyl palmitate enhances free PA levels in the serum to 173–425 μM compared to Veh-treated mice with 110–250 μM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A measuring serum PA concentrations.

claim: After LPS challenge, PA-treated mice experienced increased disease severity as indicated by their significant decline in temperature compared to Veh mice.
source: Interestingly, after LPS challenge, PA-treated mice experienced increased disease severity as indicated by their significant decline in temperature compared to Veh mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PA-treated mice exhibited enhanced mortality compared to Veh mice.
source: Similar to WD- and KD-fed mice, PA-treated mice also exhibited enhanced mortality, compared to Veh mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mice injected with PA for 0, 3, and 6 hr and then challenged with LPS did not exhibit increased disease severity or poor survival outcome.
source: Importantly, mice injected with PA for shorter time periods (0, 3, and 6 hr) and then challenged with LPS did not exhibit increased disease severity or poor survival outcome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), concluding that a 12-hr pre-treatment with PA is required for an increase in disease severity.
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature and survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: A 12-hr pre-treatment with PA is required for an increase in disease severity.
source: Importantly, mice injected with PA for shorter time periods (0, 3, and 6 hr) and then challenged with LPS did not exhibit increased disease severity or poor survival outcome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), concluding that a 12-hr pre-treatment with PA is required for an increase in disease severity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only 12-hr PA pre-treatment, but not shorter durations, enhanced disease severity.

claim: 12-hr PA-pre-treated mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Tnf at 5 hr post-LPS challenge compared to Veh control.
source: Next, we measured systemic inflammatory status during disease and found similar to KD-fed mice, the 12-hr PA-pre-treated mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Tnf (5 hr and 10 hr) and Il6 (5 hr) post-LPS challenge, compared to Veh control (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C measuring Tnf expression.

claim: 12-hr PA-pre-treated mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Tnf at 10 hr post-LPS challenge compared to Veh control.
source: Next, we measured systemic inflammatory status during disease and found similar to KD-fed mice, the 12-hr PA-pre-treated mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Tnf (5 hr and 10 hr) and Il6 (5 hr) post-LPS challenge, compared to Veh control (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C measuring Tnf expression.

claim: 12-hr PA-pre-treated mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Il6 at 5 hr post-LPS challenge compared to Veh control.
source: Next, we measured systemic inflammatory status during disease and found similar to KD-fed mice, the 12-hr PA-pre-treated mice showed significantly enhanced expression of Tnf (5 hr and 10 hr) and Il6 (5 hr) post-LPS challenge, compared to Veh control (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D measuring Il6 expression.

claim: 12-hr pre-treatment with PA did not alter LPS-induced hypoglycemia.
source: Importantly, as a control we looked at LPS-induced hypoglycemia in PA-treated mice, and 12-hr pre-treatment with PA did not alter LPS-induced hypoglycemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), indicating that diet-dependent hypoglycemic shock was not a driver of endotoxemia severity in PA-treated mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Diet-dependent hypoglycemic shock was not a driver of endotoxemia severity in PA-treated mice.
source: Importantly, as a control we looked at LPS-induced hypoglycemia in PA-treated mice, and 12-hr pre-treatment with PA did not alter LPS-induced hypoglycemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), indicating that diet-dependent hypoglycemic shock was not a driver of endotoxemia severity in PA-treated mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PA-treated and control mice showed similar hypoglycemia despite different disease outcomes.

claim: Exposure to PA to mimic systemic levels found in humans eating high-fat diets is sufficient to drive enhanced inflammation and disease severity in mice stimulated with endotoxin.
source: Thus, exposure to PA to mimic systemic levels found in humans eating high-fat diets is sufficient to drive enhanced inflammation and disease severity in mice stimulated with endotoxin, and this effect is dependent on length of PA exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that PA injection enhanced inflammation and disease severity in a time-dependent manner.

claim: The effect of PA on enhanced inflammation and disease severity is dependent on length of PA exposure.
source: Thus, exposure to PA to mimic systemic levels found in humans eating high-fat diets is sufficient to drive enhanced inflammation and disease severity in mice stimulated with endotoxin, and this effect is dependent on length of PA exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 12-hr but not shorter PA exposures enhanced disease severity.

claim: Trained immunity is induced when a primary inflammatory stimulus changes transcription of inflammatory genes, the immune status returns to basal levels, and challenge with a secondary stimulus enhances transcription of inflammatory cytokines at much higher levels than those observed during the primary challenge.
source: Importantly, trained immunity is induced when a primary inflammatory stimulus changes transcription of inflammatory genes, the immune status returns to basal levels, and challenge with a secondary stimulus enhances transcription of inflammatory cytokines at much higher levels than those observed during the primary challenge (Divangahi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Divangahi et al., 2021).

claim: Basal levels of Tnf, Il6, Il1b, and Il10 in the blood of mice pre-exposed to PA were comparable to control mice immediately prior to endotoxin challenge.
source: While the dynamics of an initial inflammatory event induced by PA in vivo are not defined in this paper, we show that basal levels of Tnf, Il6, Il1b, and Il10 in the blood of mice pre-exposed to PA were comparable to control mice immediately prior to endotoxin challenge, indicating that mice were not in a primed state prior to disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F measuring baseline cytokine expression.

claim: Mice pre-exposed to PA were not in a primed state prior to disease.
source: While the dynamics of an initial inflammatory event induced by PA in vivo are not defined in this paper, we show that basal levels of Tnf, Il6, Il1b, and Il10 in the blood of mice pre-exposed to PA were comparable to control mice immediately prior to endotoxin challenge, indicating that mice were not in a primed state prior to disease.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that baseline cytokine levels were similar between PA-treated and control mice.

claim: The hyper-inflammation and poor disease outcome in PA-exposed mice are not due to priming but a trained immune response.
source: This suggests that the hyper-inflammation and poor disease outcome we show in PA-exposed mice are not due to priming but a trained immune response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PA-exposed mice showed normal baseline inflammation but enhanced responses to secondary challenge.

claim: When challenged with systemic LPS, PA→SC mice showed an increase in disease severity compared to Veh→SC mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: When challenged with systemic LPS, PA→SC mice showed an increase in mortality compared to Veh→SC mice.

claim: PA alone can induce long-lived trained immunity that increases susceptibility to inflammatory disease.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PA exposure followed by a 7-day rest period still enhanced disease severity.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012).

claim: Rag1−/− mice treated with PA for 12 hr showed a significant decrease in kidney fungal burden compared to Veh mice, 24 hr post-C. albicans infection.
source: In accordance with canonical trained immunity models, mice treated with PA for 12 hr showed a significant decrease in kidney fungal burden compared to Veh mice, 24 hr post-infection (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU quantification data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: PA enhances innate immune clearance of C. albicans in vivo.
source: These are the first data to suggest PA enhances innate immune clearance of C. albicans in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PA-treated Rag1−/− mice (lacking adaptive immunity) showed reduced fungal burden.

claim: OA (C18:1) is a mono-unsaturated fatty acid naturally found in animal fats and vegetable oils.

evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about OA.

claim: In the presence of PA, OA diverts lipid metabolism away from ceramide production.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Palomer et al., 2018).

claim: Systemic OA can abrogate KD-dependent hypothermia in response to LPS in mice-fed diets enriched solely in SFA.

claim: Systemic OA can abrogate KD-dependent survival defect in response to LPS in mice-fed diets enriched solely in SFA.

claim: KD alters the composition of the hematopoietic stem cell compartment.

claim: Lipidomics identified enhanced PA-associated lipids in KD-fed mice serum.

claim: Pre-treatment with physiologically relevant concentrations of PA induces a hyper-inflammatory response to LPS in macrophages.

evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that ceramide synthase inhibition reduced PA-induced hyper-inflammation.

claim: Systemic PA confers enhanced inflammation in response to systemic LPS.

claim: Systemic PA confers enhanced mortality in response to systemic LPS.
source: In vivo, we found systemic PA confers enhanced inflammation and mortality in response to systemic LPS, and this phenotype was not reversible for up to 7 days post-PA-exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data showing increased mortality in PA-treated mice after LPS challenge.

claim: The phenotype of enhanced inflammation and mortality in response to systemic LPS was not reversible for up to 7 days post-PA-exposure.
source: In vivo, we found systemic PA confers enhanced inflammation and mortality in response to systemic LPS, and this phenotype was not reversible for up to 7 days post-PA-exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that mice rested for 7 days after PA exposure still showed enhanced disease severity.

claim: PA exposure enhanced clearance of Candida albicans in Rag1-/- mice.

claim: Oleic acid reverses PA-induced enhanced mortality in response to LPS.

claim: There is plasticity of innate immune reprogramming by dietary constituents.
